title: The Acts of the Apostles
lead: The New Testament's account of the first thirty years of the church, from Jesus' ascension in Jerusalem (Acts 1) to Paul preaching in Rome under guard (Acts 28). It is the second volume of a two-part work addressed to Theophilus; the first is the Gospel of Luke (Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1). This page is about the book: its author, date, purpose, genre, its two forms of text, and how it relates to Paul's letters.

sections.b: Acts opens by pointing back to "my first book" and picks up where Luke's Gospel ends: the risen Jesus tells his followers to wait in Jerusalem for power from on high, then he is taken up (Luke 24:49–53; Acts 1:4–11). Most scholars, following Henry Cadbury, read Luke and Acts as one work, often called Luke-Acts. Jesus' journey to Jerusalem and his trials are mirrored by Paul's journey to Jerusalem and his trials, and the promise of Acts 1:8, that the apostles will be witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth, gives the book its plan.

The book names no author. From the late 100s (Irenaeus, the Muratorian Fragment) the church named Luke, the doctor who traveled with Paul (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11), and the "we" passages (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16) seem to put the writer at Paul's side. Many critical scholars think instead of an unknown admirer of Paul writing a generation later. Dates proposed run from about AD 62, when the story stops, through AD 80–90, the most common view, to about AD 110–120 (Richard Pervo, Joseph Tyson).
sections.refs: Acts 16:10–17; Acts 20:5–15; Acts 21:1–18; Acts 27:1–28:16; Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11

sections.b: Acts survives in two main forms. The text in most modern Bibles rests on manuscripts such as Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus. The "Western" text, best known from Codex Bezae (about AD 400), is about 8.5 percent longer and adds many vivid details. Scholars still debate whether one form revised the other, or whether, as Friedrich Blass proposed, Luke himself issued two editions. Most think the shorter text is closer to the original.
